passage: Last week Vijay called me "Speedy Gonzales" because I run fast in PT class. I laughed so hard my water bottle fell. Then he did it again at lunch, and I laughed again, and Vijay did a little bow. It felt like our secret club joke. But when Rohan from the next bench said, "Preeti, why is your lunchbox always the same dal-roti?" I went quiet and stared at the steel dabba. Rohan kept grinning and repeated it. Vijay noticed my face before I said anything. He said, "Arre Rohan, that's not funny, stop." I still felt hot in my ears. I'm not sure whether Rohan meant harm.

qa.q: What nickname did Vijay give Preeti in PT class?
qa.a: Vijay called her "Speedy Gonzales" because she runs fast in PT class.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when Rohan asked about her lunchbox, and what else might explain her silence?
qa.a: Most likely she felt embarrassed and hurt, shown by going quiet, staring at the dabba and her hot ears. She might also have been unsure how to answer, since Rohan was grinning and may not have meant harm.

qa.q: What could Preeti try next time someone teases her about something sore?
qa.a: She could say calmly, "I don't like that joke," or tell Vijay or a teacher afterwards. Speaking up early makes it easier for the teaser to stop.

qa.q: How might Rohan see the lunchbox comment, compared with Preeti?
qa.a: Rohan may think it was harmless banter like Vijay's nickname, so he keeps grinning. He may not realise the topic was a sore spot for her until he sees her quiet face.

grounding: Shows the same teasing style as fun with Vijay (both laugh, safe topic) and hurtful with Rohan (sore spot, continues after silence).

passage: Teacher's note, Class 5. During the group activity today Zainab and Rehana were paired. Rehana kept saying "Zainab the sleepy tortoise" about her slow start, and both girls giggled, so I let it pass. Later a third child added a comment about Zainab's stammer while reading aloud. Zainab looked at her shoes, her smile went flat, and she stopped taking part. The other child continued for a few seconds. I walked over, asked Zainab quietly whether she wanted to step outside with me, and reminded the group that jokes stop when someone goes quiet. I will check in with Zainab tomorrow and speak with the other child privately. 🙂

qa.q: Who was paired for the group activity in Class 5?
qa.a: Zainab and Rehana were paired for the group activity.

qa.q: What did Zainab's flat smile and looking at her shoes suggest she felt, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It most likely suggests she felt hurt or embarrassed about the comment on her stammer. It could also mean she was tired or overwhelmed, so the teacher checks in rather than assuming.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to support Zainab after this?
qa.a: The teacher can check in with Zainab tomorrow, speak privately with the child who made the comment, and keep reminding the class that jokes stop when someone goes quiet.

qa.q: Why might Rehana's tortoise joke feel different to Zainab than the stammer comment?
qa.a: Zainab laughed along with Rehana's joke, so it felt shared and safe. The stammer comment pointed at something she may already feel sensitive about.

grounding: Contrasts affectionate teasing where both laugh with teasing that hit a sore spot and continued after distress, with a teacher checking in.

passage: "Beta, listen to this one," said Naveen, setting down his tea. "When I was your age, in Class 6, we had a maths teacher who never smiled. One day I asked him, 'Sir, why was six afraid of seven?' He said nothing. I said, 'Because seven eight nine!' The whole class exploded. Even Sir's moustache twitched. After that I collected riddles in a notebook and told one at every recess. The boys who used to ignore me started saving me a seat." Suraj groaned, then grinned. "Dadu, that's the same joke you told last Diwali!" "Good jokes never retire," Naveen said, and started another.

qa.q: What did young Naveen ask his maths teacher?
qa.a: He asked, "Sir, why was six afraid of seven?" and gave the answer, "Because seven eight nine!"

qa.q: What did Naveen want when he began collecting riddles in a notebook?
qa.a: He seems to have wanted to share fun and belong, since he told one at every recess and the boys who ignored him began saving him a seat.

qa.q: What could Suraj do to try his own wordplay with his grandfather?
qa.a: Suraj could invent a pun of his own, or trade riddles with Naveen at teatime, so the two of them can enjoy a new joke together.

qa.q: How might the strict teacher have seen Naveen's joke?
qa.a: His moustache twitched, so he may have been amused even though he never smiled. He might also have been surprised that a quiet boy dared to joke with him.

grounding: An elder recalls how a school-age child's pun and riddle habit showed playful language awareness and a wish to be part of the group.

passage: The power cut hit during the school bus breakdown, and thirty kids sat sweating in the dark on the roadside. Divyansh could hear Class 4 getting restless. "Okay, riddle time," he called, torch pointing at his own chin. "What has hands but can't clap?" Silence. Then Mohit yelled, "A clock!" and the whole row cheered. "What's a cat's favourite colour?" "Purr-ple!" someone shouted, and even the conductor laughed. Divyansh's voice had gone hoarse, but he kept the puns coming until the replacement bus arrived, and Mohit kept clapping for each one. 😄

qa.q: What was the answer Mohit shouted to the riddle about hands?
qa.a: Mohit shouted, "A clock!"

qa.q: What was Divyansh probably feeling as he kept telling puns in the dark?
qa.a: He was probably enjoying the shared fun and wanting to keep the group cheerful, shown by his continuing until his voice went hoarse. He might also have been a little nervous himself and used jokes to calm down.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do if his voice gives out before the bus arrives?
qa.a: He could hand the torch to Mohit or another child to ask the next riddle, so the game continues and everyone joins in.

qa.q: How might Mohit and the other children feel about the riddles during the wait?
qa.a: The riddles turn a long, sweaty wait into a game, so Mohit and the others probably feel less restless and more like one group.

grounding: A school-age child uses puns and riddles under a constraint (power cut, broken-down bus) to share fun and hold the group together.

passage: Hrithik's uncle Pankaj came back from the fields, wiping his face. "Ufff, it's raining cats and dogs. Bring the cattle in." Hrithik ran to the door, looked up at the sky and looked down at the mud. Not one cat, not one dog. He turned around, puzzled. "Kaka, where are the cats?" Pankaj burst out laughing. "Arre, it just means very heavy rain. Like we say, 'moosladhaar barish.'" Hrithik frowned, then tried it on his cousin: "Bahut heavy hai, cats and dogs!" Pankaj slapped his knee. "You'll be a teacher yet," he said.

qa.q: What did Pankaj say when he came back from the fields?
qa.a: He said, "Ufff, it's raining cats and dogs. Bring the cattle in."

qa.q: Why did Hrithik look at the sky and the mud, and what was he thinking?
qa.a: He took the phrase literally and was searching for actual cats and dogs, so he was puzzled. Once Pankaj explained it, his frown suggests he was working out a new meaning.

qa.q: What would help a child who takes an idiom literally?
qa.a: An adult can explain what the phrase means, then compare it with a similar saying in the child's own language, as Pankaj did with 'moosladhaar barish'.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Hrithik's question?
qa.a: Pankaj finds it funny and endearing rather than silly, since he laughs, explains kindly and praises Hrithik for trying the phrase himself.

grounding: A school-age child takes an idiom literally at first, then learns its figurative meaning through a warm explanation and a local equivalent.

passage: At the Istanbul language club, Lars stood at the front and said, "Let's break the ice with a game." Selin, nine years old and new in the country, glanced at the frozen pond photo on the wall. She raised her hand. "Why we break ice? Is it dangerous?" A few children giggled; her cheeks turned pink. Lars crouched down beside her chair. "Good question. In English it means starting a friendly talk when people don't know each other. Do you have a saying like that in Turkish?" Selin thought and whispered a phrase about melting the snow between people. "Same idea!" Lars said, and she smiled with relief. 🙂

qa.q: Where did Lars say "Let's break the ice with a game"?
qa.a: He said it at the Istanbul language club.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling when the children giggled, and what else might explain her pink cheeks?
qa.a: She likely felt embarrassed, since her cheeks turned pink after the giggles. It could also be shyness about speaking in a new language in front of everyone.

qa.q: What could Lars or the other children do to help Selin with idioms she hasn't met?
qa.a: They could explain the meaning simply, invite her to share a similar saying from her own language, and make it clear that asking is welcome.

qa.q: How might the children who giggled see Selin's question?
qa.a: They may have found the literal question funny without meaning to hurt, since they already know the idiom. Seeing Lars answer kindly could help them see it as a real learning moment.

grounding: A child learning an idiom in a second language takes it literally and needs cultural explanation, which is supplied with a comparison.

subtype: Simile and metaphor in writing and speech [Expressing]
passage: Mehak was sitting two desks behind Disha in Hindi class when the writing task began. Disha chewed her pencil for a long time, staring out at the neem tree. Then she wrote quickly, tongue slightly out. When the teacher asked who wanted to read, Disha's hand went up before anyone else's, which surprised Mehak. "The moon is a silver coin somebody dropped in the puddle of night," she read. Her voice shook slightly on "puddle". Mehak noticed she was smiling at the paper, not at the class. The teacher said nothing for a moment, then asked, "What made you think of a coin?" Disha shrugged, pleased.

qa.q: Which tree was Disha staring at while she chewed her pencil?
qa.a: She was staring out at the neem tree.

qa.q: What might Disha have been feeling as she read her line aloud, and what else could her shaking voice mean?
qa.a: She probably felt proud and a little exposed, shown by her raised hand, her smile at the paper and pleased shrug. The slight shake might also just be nerves about reading aloud.

qa.q: How could the teacher encourage Disha to keep writing figurative lines?
qa.a: The teacher could ask about her images, as she did, and invite Disha to try another comparison for a mood or feeling she finds hard to name.

qa.q: How does Mehak see Disha's reading?
qa.a: Mehak is surprised because Disha is not usually first to volunteer, and she notices Disha's smile. From Mehak's view, the line seems to matter personally to Disha.

grounding: An observer describes a child's metaphor 'The moon is a silver coin', which shows imagination and an attempt to express a feeling.

subtype: Simile and metaphor in writing and speech [Expressing]
passage:
Monday. Dhruv handed his notebook to Manoj, the Class 5 teacher, with his eyes on the floor. It said only, "The rain was wet." Manoj smiled and asked how the rain felt on the way to school. Dhruv shrugged. "Like drums, I think."

Thursday. Manoj read out a line by another child, "as quiet as a mouse." Dhruv wrote it down and next to it added, "as loud as my brother's cricket bat." He showed it to Manoj without being asked.

Two weeks later. Dhruv's page read, "When I lost the match, my chest was a heavy bag of wet sand." He grinned when Manoj said, "That says a lot." 🙂

qa.q: What did Dhruv's first sentence say on Monday?
qa.a: His notebook said only, "The rain was wet."

qa.q: What was Dhruv likely feeling when he wrote about the heavy bag of wet sand, and what else might it hint?
qa.a: He likely felt disappointed about losing the match, and figurative words gave him a way to say it. It might also show he was relaxed enough with Manoj to share feelings he could not name directly.

qa.q: What might Manoj do next to keep building Dhruv's confidence in writing?
qa.a: Manoj could keep asking how things felt, share short similes from other children, and praise Dhruv's own images without correcting every detail.

qa.q: How would things be different for Dhruv if Manoj had only said the first sentence was too plain?
qa.a: Dhruv might have kept his eyes down and stayed with flat sentences. Manoj's curious question instead led him to find his own words.

grounding: Over three beats a child moves from flat writing to similes and metaphors that carry feelings lacking direct words.

passage: The temple hall was jammed for the evening bhajan, and the microphone kept crackling. Yamini, ten, stood near the back next to her cousin Vaibhav, who could barely hear the harmonium. "I can't hear the words," he whispered. "Just listen to the clapping," Yamini said. She started clapping on the beat, a little late at first, then found it. By the third verse she was singing the refrain along with the ladies at the front. Her shoulders loosened. Vaibhav mouthed the words a half-beat behind, looking around instead of closing his eyes. "It doesn't do much for me," he admitted afterwards. "But you looked happy."

qa.q: Who was standing next to Yamini in the temple hall?
qa.a: Her cousin Vaibhav was standing next to her.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel while singing the refrain, and how do we know?
qa.a: She seems calm and happy, since her shoulders loosened and she sang along by the third verse. Vaibhav's different reaction shows the feeling isn't the same for everyone.

qa.q: What could Yamini do to help Vaibhav feel included if the singing doesn't move him?
qa.a: She could let him join in the clapping, or simply accept that he can enjoy the evening in his own way without needing to feel what she feels.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav experience the bhajan?
qa.a: Vaibhav struggles to hear the words and doesn't feel much, although he notices Yamini looked happy. He stays polite and honest about it.

grounding: A child joins devotional singing where rhythm and shared voice bring calm and belonging, while another child's experience differs.

passage: Every Sunday morning the Pnar hymn circle met in the church basement in Shillong, and Lalremsiami, nine, always stood beside Shalini, who came with her neighbour. Lalremsiami loved the part where the voices rose all together. Today the choir sang "Bless the Lord" and she closed her eyes; the hum in her chest felt like being carried. Beside her, Shalini kept her eyes open, counting the ceiling tiles, but tapped her foot to the beat. Afterwards over tea, Lalremsiami asked, "Did you like it?" "The tune is nice," Shalini said. "I like when everyone breathes together." Lalremsiami nodded. "That's my favourite part too." 🎶

qa.q: Where did the hymn circle meet on Sunday mornings?
qa.a: The hymn circle met in the church basement in Shillong.

qa.q: What did the hum in her chest suggest about how Lalremsiami felt during the hymn?
qa.a: It suggests she felt calm and carried by the shared voices, with closed eyes as evidence. Shalini's open eyes show that another child may feel something quite different.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami do if she wants to invite Shalini again without pressure?
qa.a: She could ask again warmly, let Shalini join in whichever way she likes, and talk about what Shalini enjoys, like everyone breathing together.

qa.q: How does Shalini experience the same hymn?
qa.a: Shalini enjoys the tune and the shared breathing but stays watchful, counting tiles. Her joy is quieter and shows through her tapping foot.

grounding: A child joins group hymns where shared voice brings calm and belonging, and a companion's different experience is respected.

passage: Akash's grandfather had died on Tuesday. Aparna, the girl next door, watched from her balcony as relatives filled the courtyard in white clothes. Akash, seven, stood near the door with a paper aeroplane in his hand. When the priest began chanting, he asked his mother something in a whisper, and she hugged him tight. After a while Aparna saw him crouch beside a plant and fold the aeroplane again. An aunty called him for a prayer and he went quietly, looking at the floor. Later he was on the stairs, giggling with a cousin over a torn kite. Then he stopped, frowned, and went back inside.

qa.q: What was Akash holding when he stood near the door?
qa.a: He was holding a paper aeroplane.

qa.q: What might Akash have been feeling when he folded the aeroplane and later giggled, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: He may have felt sad and confused, and play gave him a short break from it. It could also be that he was simply restless or did not fully understand what the rites meant.

qa.q: How could an adult support Akash in the days after the funeral?
qa.a: An adult could answer his questions simply and honestly, let him play between sad moments, and be nearby when he wants to talk.

qa.q: How does Aparna see Akash's day?
qa.a: Aparna, watching from her balcony, sees a boy moving between sadness and play. She may not know what he really feels inside.

grounding: A child observes family mourning through prayers and gatherings and moves between grief and play, as an observer sees.

passage:
Day one. After the funeral of her grandmother, Kavitha, eight, sat under the dining table. "Where did Ajji go?" she asked Shalini, her aunt. Shalini knelt down. "Her body stopped working and she died. We won't see her again, but we can remember her." Kavitha nodded and asked for a biscuit.

Day four. Kavitha sat quietly through the evening prayer, holding Shalini's hand. Afterwards she ran to play with the neighbour's children.

Day nine. Kavitha lit an oil lamp near Ajji's photo and stayed silent for a while. "I miss her hands," she said. Shalini held her. 🤍

qa.q: What did Kavitha ask Shalini on the first day?
qa.a: She asked, "Where did Ajji go?"

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she asked for a biscuit after hearing about death, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: She may have taken in the answer and needed something ordinary and comforting. It could also mean she had not fully absorbed it yet, which is common for children who grieve in short bursts.

qa.q: What could Shalini keep doing to help Kavitha?
qa.a: Shalini can keep answering honestly and simply, let Kavitha play between sad moments, and stay close when Kavitha wants to remember her grandmother.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel while answering Kavitha's questions?
qa.a: Shalini is grieving too, so it may be hard to speak steadily. She still kneels down and answers gently.

grounding: A child sees a family mourn, asks what death means, and grieves in short bursts with simple honest answers over several days.

passage: Tuesday, 8 pm. Aditi's diary. Today Ishita gave me my name sign at last! It's a tiny circle by my ear, because of my earring, and everybody in the Deaf club clapped their hands in the air. Before that I always fingerspelled A-D-I-T-I, all five letters, and it made me feel slow. Ishita said the name sign is how people will call me from across the room now. I practised A-D-I-T-I with my fingers on the bus anyway. Fingerspelling is for new words, like when Sir taught us the sign for "volcano" and we didn't know the letters. I want to teach Amma my name sign tomorrow. 😊

qa.q: What is Aditi's name sign made of?
qa.a: It is a tiny circle by the ear, because of the earring.

qa.q: How does Aditi feel about getting her name sign, and what else might she feel about fingerspelling?
qa.a: Aditi feels happy and included, shown by the excitement and the plan to teach Amma. Fingerspelling the name also felt slow, so the sign relieves that.

qa.q: What could Aditi do next to keep learning?
qa.a: Aditi could keep practising fingerspelling for names and new words while using the name sign in the club, and ask Ishita for help with signs that are unknown.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel about giving Aditi the name sign?
qa.a: Ishita probably feels glad to welcome Aditi into the community, since Ishita explained how the sign will help people call Aditi across the room.

grounding: A young signer receives a community name sign and understands fingerspelling as a tool within a full language.

passage: On market day the little bus stop in Kalimpong was crowded, and Aparna, ten, watched her deaf friend Akash bargain for a pencil box. The shopkeeper didn't sign, so Akash pointed and wrote the price on his palm. Then he saw another friend, Prem, across the lane and made a quick shape with his right hand on his chest, his name sign. Prem grinned and signed back. When Aparna wanted to introduce her cousin "Tashi", Akash slowly fingerspelled T-A-S-H-I, then asked for a name sign idea. The others laughed and suggested a hand shape like a mountain. Akash gave Tashi a thumbs up. "That's it."

qa.q: Where was the crowded bus stop?
qa.a: It was in Kalimpong.

qa.q: What was Akash likely feeling when the others gave Tashi a name sign, and what other reading is possible?
qa.a: He probably felt friendly and included, as he gave Tashi a thumbs up. He might also have been making sure Tashi belonged since a name sign is given by the community.

qa.q: What could Aparna do to help Tashi learn signs for his own name?
qa.a: She could ask Akash and Prem to teach Tashi the mountain sign, and practise fingerspelling T-A-S-H-I together so he can use both.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper see Akash's way of buying the pencil box?
qa.a: The shopkeeper may have found it different, but Akash still managed. The scene shows how communication can work through pointing and writing.

grounding: A school-age signer fingerspells a new name and uses community name signs, showing fingerspelling as part of a fuller language.

passage: Friday. Nirmala's diary. Today in Tenzin's class I forgot to look at Sir when he signed, and looked at my book instead. Tenzin tapped my shoulder twice and waited. I felt hot because it seemed rude, but he only smiled and pointed at his eyes. He explained that in sign language you keep looking at the signer's hands and face the whole time, and looking away means you are not listening. Then he flicked the lights to get everyone's attention when Mr Rao came in. It's clever! Tomorrow I'm going to keep my eyes up even when my pencil drops. 🙂

qa.q: How did Tenzin get Nirmala's attention?
qa.a: Tenzin tapped Nirmala's shoulder twice and waited.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when Tenzin tapped her shoulder, and what did she learn?
qa.a: Nirmala felt embarrassed, thinking it was rude, shown by feeling hot. Then Nirmala learned that keeping eyes on the signer is expected, not an insult.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do next time her pencil drops during a signed lesson?
qa.a: Nirmala could keep watching the signer, then pick the pencil up at a pause or ask quietly by signing 'wait' before looking away.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Nirmala's mistake?
qa.a: Tenzin is kind about it. Tenzin smiles and points to the eyes, treating it as something Nirmala has not learned yet.

grounding: A young learner discovers that visual attention and turn-taking, like tapping and flicking lights, are respectful and required in signing.

passage: The village school at Sundarpur had one hearing teacher and Wasim, a deaf Class 6 boy, at the third bench. Devika, ten, had just moved to the village. When the teacher began to explain fractions, Devika saw that Wasim's eyes never left the interpreter's hands. When the teacher called him, she waved to get his attention, and he turned with a smile. At break she said, "Why do you stare at her so much?" Wasim signed slowly, and the interpreter translated: "It is how I listen." Devika nodded. "Then I'll wave before I talk."

qa.q: Which bench did Wasim sit at?
qa.a: He sat at the third bench.

qa.q: What did Devika probably feel when Wasim explained why he stared at the interpreter, and what other reaction is possible?
qa.a: She probably felt understanding and a little embarrassed for asking. She might also have felt a bit unsure about how to talk to him, though she decided on waving first.

qa.q: What could Devika do to be a good friend to Wasim?
qa.a: She could wave or tap gently before speaking, look at him when he signs, and learn a few signs so they can talk directly.

qa.q: What might it be like for Wasim when a new classmate asks about his staring?
qa.a: He may be patient since he explained in his own language. He might feel glad she listens, or tired of explaining again.

grounding: A signer keeps eye gaze on the signer's hands and face, and a new classmate learns to gain attention by waving.

passage: Thursday night. Dear Diary, Kamal here. Today I gave Rukmini a note. It said, "Thank you for sharing your tiffin when I forgot mine. You are my best friend." I couldn't say it in her face, my mouth got stuck. She read it in the corridor and put it in her pencil box, and didn't say anything, but she smiled all the way to class. Chhoti Didi tried to read this diary earlier, so I hid it behind my school shoes. I don't like it when people read my diary. I will keep writing here. Tomorrow I'll write a thank-you letter to Nani too. 🙂

qa.q: What did Kamal write in the note to Rukmini?
qa.a: Kamal wrote, "Thank you for sharing your tiffin when I forgot mine. You are my best friend."

qa.q: Why did Kamal write the note instead of saying it to Rukmini?
qa.a: Kamal felt their mouth got stuck, so writing was easier for a feeling that was hard to say aloud. Kamal may also have felt shy about Rukmini's reaction.

qa.q: What could Kamal do about Chhoti Didi trying to read the diary?
qa.a: Kamal could tell Chhoti Didi calmly that the diary is private, or ask a parent to help set a rule about respecting each other's diaries.

qa.q: How does Rukmini feel about the note?
qa.a: Rukmini says nothing but smiles all the way to class and keeps the note in her pencil box, so she seems touched, though she may be shy too.

grounding: A child writes a thank-you note and a diary to share feelings hard to say aloud, and wants the diary's privacy respected.

passage: Zeenat sat on the charpai under the mango tree with a pencil and a torn page. Her friend Dilnaz was going away to her uncle's town for the whole summer, and Zeenat didn't know what to say. She wrote: "Dear Dilnaz, I will miss playing kho-kho with you. Please write to me." Then she crossed out "miss" and wrote "really miss". She folded it small and tucked it into Dilnaz's school bag while she wasn't looking. Later she saw Dilnaz pull it out on the bullock cart, read it twice, and press it to her chest. Zeenat looked away and pretended to count the coconut trees. ❤️

qa.q: Where did Zeenat sit while writing the letter?
qa.a: She sat on the charpai under the mango tree.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she crossed out "miss" and wrote "really miss", and what else might explain her looking away later?
qa.a: She felt sad about the separation and wanted her feelings to show clearly on paper. She looked away perhaps because she was shy watching Dilnaz read something so personal.

qa.q: What could Zeenat and Dilnaz do to keep their friendship going over the summer?
qa.a: They could write letters to each other, share small news from their days, and plan a game to play when Dilnaz returns.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel when she reads the letter on the bullock cart?
qa.a: She probably feels touched and cared for, since she reads it twice and presses it to her chest, though she might also feel sad about leaving.

grounding: A school-age child writes a note to a friend, sharing feelings that are hard to say aloud.

passage: In the school's Creative Writing Club at 4 pm, Kunal read his story out loud to Samir, the club teacher. It was about a fox called Bhuri who lost her voice. "'I can't sing,' whispered Bhuri. 'Then we'll sing for you,' said the crows." Kunal's cheeks were warm and he kept his eyes on the page. Samir smiled. "That last line stayed with me. Is Bhuri sad?" Kunal thought. "A bit. But she has friends." Samir didn't ask whether it was about Kunal. He only said, "Stories can hold feelings. Thank you for sharing it." Kunal nodded, relieved, and added a poem about his dog. 🙂

qa.q: What was the fox in Kunal's story called?
qa.a: The fox was called Bhuri.

qa.q: What did Kunal's warm cheeks and eyes on the page suggest he felt, and what else might they mean?
qa.a: They suggest he felt shy and a little exposed reading his own work aloud. They might also mean excitement about sharing it.

qa.q: What could Samir do next to support Kunal's writing?
qa.a: Samir could keep responding to the story as a story, ask what happens next to Bhuri, and let Kunal decide whether to share anything about himself.

qa.q: What does Samir's decision not to ask 'Is it about you?' do for Kunal?
qa.a: It lets Kunal keep his story as fiction, so he can share feelings safely without being asked to explain or being pinned to a real event.

grounding: A child writes a story with dialogue and a poem; fiction can carry feelings, but the teacher treats it as a story and not literal fact.

passage: Ganga's little brother Farhan had a habit of writing in a notebook beside the fruit stall. Ganga, watching from the stall, saw him scribble a poem: "My cat Moti ran away / and the sky went grey." Then he wrote a story where a boy shouted at his teacher and flew away on a dragon. Their mother read over his shoulder and looked worried. "Did Farhan shout at his teacher?" she asked Ganga. Ganga shook her head. "No, it's a story, Ammi. He got a dragon in it." Farhan looked up, grinning, and read out the dragon's growl. Their mother relaxed and laughed.

qa.q: What was the name of the cat in Farhan's poem?
qa.a: The cat in Farhan's poem was named Moti.

qa.q: Why did Farhan's mother look worried, and what else could she have thought?
qa.a: She may have worried that the story meant Farhan really shouted at his teacher. Ganga's calm answer shows another reading: the story could just be imagination.

qa.q: What could Ganga or her mother do if they do want to know how Farhan feels about school?
qa.a: They could ask him gently about his day, without treating the dragon story as proof of what happened, and listen to what he says.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when his mother asks whether he shouted at his teacher?
qa.a: He may feel misunderstood or surprised, since it was a made-up story. He seems proud enough of it to read out the dragon's growl.

grounding: A child writes stories and poems; fiction can carry real feelings, but a story is not proof that events or wishes are literal.
